title: Guard the mind
hookLine: a list of resolutions broken by noon; Shantideva says guard one thing, the mind, and the rest are kept
carry: guard the mind with the rope of mindfulness
tomorrow: nobody can cover the whole earth in leather. so what can you do?

cards: No phone at dinner. No snacks after nine. Be kinder to your brother.
Drink more water. Answer emails the same day. A list of good rules taped to the fridge, and by noon on Monday half of them are already broken.

Each rule needs its own guard, and there aren't enough guards. So, yesterday's question: is there one guard that keeps them all? Shantideva says yes, and he puts it in the very first verse of his new chapter.

teach.h: GUARD THE MIND, KEEP THE TRAINING.
teach.b: Whoever wants to guard their training, he says, must guard the mind with great care; let the mind go unguarded, and the training can't be kept. Then a picture.
An untamed mind is like a wild elephant, doing more harm than any elephant in a rage. But tie that elephant with the rope of mindfulness, and fears fall away and good things follow.
So the one guard is attention itself, checking in: where is my mind right now, and what is it about to do? Neighbors know this teaching.

teach.h: KEEP THY HEART WITH ALL DILIGENCE.
teach.b: The book of Proverbs, in the Jewish and Christian Bible, says in the King James English: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life."
Shared ground, and plenty of it: both put the inner life first, upstream of every rule, and both say keeping it takes steady effort. One honest difference.
In Proverbs, a parent hands down wisdom that begins, as the book says, in the fear of the LORD; the heart is kept by holding to God's teaching.
Shantideva's guard is the mind watching itself, mindfulness and alertness, with no creator giving the command. One heart, one mind, kept with care.

how: Buddhists train mindfulness (smriti) and alertness (samprajanya) in sitting meditation and through the day, often by pausing to check what the mind is doing; Shantideva's fifth chapter is studied as a guide to that watchfulness.

o: keeping your private thoughts hidden from others
keeping steady watch over what the mind is doing
blocking every negative thought before it arrives

games.q: one guard, two traditions — tap the pairs.
p: keep thy heart with all diligence

s: Shantideva says guarding the mind means keeping every rule separately
guard the mind, and the training is kept; one guard for all.
Proverbs also puts the inner life upstream of everything else
'for out of it are the issues of life.'
Proverbs and Shantideva mean exactly the same thing by keeping the heart or mind
both say keep it with care; in Proverbs by holding to God's teaching, in Shantideva by mindfulness and alertness.

games.q: you're starting a new job and want to be patient, honest and on time. by Shantideva's first verse of chapter five, where do you put your effort?
o: write three detailed rules and track each one in an app.
check in with your own mind through the day: where is it, what's it about to do?
wait until a problem comes up, then fix that one thing.
games.why: guard the mind, he says, and the training is kept. the rules matter, but the watchful mind is the one guard that keeps them.

practice: Choose one steady sound around you: a fan, traffic, the hum of a fridge. Rest your listening there. Each time you notice you've drifted somewhere else, simply ask, where is my mind right now, and come back to the sound.

wordCard.voice: Guard the mind: chapter five's first teaching. Keep watch over the mind, and every other promise has a keeper.

orig.note: Sanskrit: mindfulness, remembering; the 'rope' that ties the mind's elephant. Pali sati.

carryVoice: One line for the road: guard the mind with the rope of mindfulness, and the rules mostly look after themselves. Day one of chapter five.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 5.1-5.3 (to guard the training, guard the mind; the untamed mind is like a mad elephant; tied with the rope of mindfulness, fears vanish)
